title: Here’s how our climate team picked 10 promising companies to watch
gist: MIT Technology Review explains how it picked its 2026 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: the US has ceded climate-tech leadership after deregulation and incentive cuts, so the list again skews non-US (two Chinese firms: WeLion, Envision), while AI-driven electricity demand made grid energy storage (Energy Dome, Moment Energy, Form Energy) a featured sector.

insights.claim: MIT Technology Review's climate team asserts that the dismantling of US federal regulations and cuts to government innovation incentives mean the US is no longer a leader in climate tech.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Policy-driven retreat shifts climate-tech capital, talent and deployment opportunities toward non-US jurisdictions, especially China and Europe.
insights.quote: The dismembering of US federal regulations and cuts to financial government incentives for innovation means that the country is no longer a leader in climate tech.
insights.locator: The dismembering of US federal regulations

insights.claim: For the second consecutive year, the majority of companies on MIT Technology Review's climate tech watchlist are based outside the US.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A persistent geographic shift in where credible climate-tech champions are emerging, not a one-year anomaly.
insights.quote: Like last year, the 2026 list is largely composed of companies that are based outside the US.
insights.locator: The dismembering of US federal regulations

insights.claim: The editors note that political shifts and international conflict have stalled climate progress, particularly in the US, and that political will has weakened even as climate damages mount.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Climate-tech companies face a widening gap between physical need and policy support, raising reliance on pure economics and non-US markets.
insights.quote: Political will has weakened even as the damages wrought by climate change continue to mount.
insights.locator: A wide range of technologies is

insights.claim: China is described as an obvious hotspot for energy and climate innovation, with two Chinese companies on the 2026 list: WeLion (semi-solid-state EV batteries) and Envision Energy (large-scale wind and storage deployment in China and globally).
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Chinese firms are leading both next-gen battery chemistry and at-scale renewables deployment, a competitive threat to Western peers.
insights.quote: China is an obvious hotspot for technological innovation across energy and climate.
insights.locator: The dismembering of US federal regulations

themes.theme: AI power demand elevates grid storage

insights.claim: Rising electricity demand, driven in part by AI data centers, is named one of the biggest stories of the year, and energy storage is framed as a key piece because it smooths supply variability as grids add renewables.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The AI power-demand narrative is now pulling capital and attention toward grid storage, not just generation.
insights.quote: One of the biggest stories of the year is the rising demand for electricity, driven in part by AI data centers.
insights.locator: The dismembering of US federal regulations

insights.claim: Three storage companies made the 2026 list with distinct approaches: Energy Dome (long-duration storage using compressed CO2), Moment Energy (repurposing EV batteries for grid storage, Canada), and Form Energy (multi-day iron-based batteries, a repeat from 2024).
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Long-duration and second-life storage are the technology bets editors see as most relevant to the AI-load and renewables-integration problem.
insights.quote: Form Energy, which we also included in the 2024 edition of this list, is producing iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days.
insights.locator: The dismembering of US federal regulations

insights.claim: A related MIT Technology Review piece notes that huge grid-scale batteries are thriving in the US while smaller residential systems have lagged.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Utility-scale storage is outpacing behind-the-meter residential storage, favoring grid-scale suppliers.
insights.quote: Huge grid-scale batteries are thriving, but smaller residential systems have lagged.

insights.claim: The selection process sources nominations from reporters, editors, academics, researchers, investors and analysts, then vets technology and business via literature, reports and patents, favoring companies with a track record in research, capital raised or deployments.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The list filters for de-risked companies with traction rather than pure early-stage bets, making it a reasonable screen for investable climate names.
insights.quote: We focus on companies that have established a track record, whether through research findings, capital raised, or deployments.
insights.locator: In this project, we look for

insights.claim: Companies are judged partly on portfolio fit: the slate is balanced across industries, geographies, development stages, returning vs. new names, and the year's major trends.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: List inclusion reflects editorial balancing, so absence does not necessarily signal weakness and inclusion is partly thematic.
insights.quote: We judge each company not only on its own merits, but also on how it might fit into our list overall.

insights.claim: The editors say technology alone cannot solve climate change, and the list covers both emissions reduction and adaptation to extreme heat, drought and flooding, ranging from mobile flood barriers to next-generation nuclear reactors.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Adaptation technologies are gaining equal billing with mitigation as warming impacts intensify.
insights.quote: Technology alone can’t solve climate change.
